_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: The benefit of discretion is his: of the one separating [the teruma], who can give it to any priest he wishes. And if an Israelite said to him, “Here is this sela, and give it to my daughter’s son, a priest,” that sela belongs to the one who separated it and not to the one for whom it was separated; and the other cannot argue that since it was separated for his own untithed produce, it turns out he is being paid a sela for what is his own. This statement of Rabbi Abbahu contains three matters.
gershom:a1.1: The benefit of discretion is his: for he may accept a zuz or a sela from his fellow Israelite in order to give it to his daughter’s son, a priest.
rashi:a2.1: There, it comes by force of an Israelite: for an Israelite set it aside. For this reason we follow the one achieving atonement, since its beginning and its end are in the hands of an Israelite, who is included in [the realm of] punishments.
gershom:a2.1: And Rami bar Ḥama: holds that in any case you cannot resolve [the dilemma] from what Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, that the one achieving atonement can effect substitution. For there, this one achieving atonement comes by force of an Israelite, whose own offering can effect substitution; that is, an Israelite consecrated it for an Israelite to achieve atonement. But where a gentile consecrated it for an Israelite to achieve atonement, so that it was not in the possession of that one achieving atonement from beginning to end, can the one achieving atonement effect substitution or not? Let it stand [teiku].
rashi:a2.2: This is the reading: “But here, this is how he raises the dilemma: Do we require from beginning to end that it stand in the possession of one who effects substitution?” That is: but here, where a gentile consecrated it for an Israelite to achieve atonement, do we require that from the beginning of the consecration to its end it stand in the possession of a person fit to effect substitution, such as an Israelite? Then this animal, since the beginning of its sanctity came by force of a gentile, cannot be substituted, even though the one achieving atonement is an Israelite. Or perhaps, since at the end it comes into the hands of the one achieving atonement, who is fit to effect substitution, the sanctity of substitution takes hold of it. Let it stand [teiku].
tosafot:a3.1: One may not benefit, by rabbinic law: Rabbi Yaakov asked: Why must we say this is rabbinic? Perhaps it is by Torah law, since we include gentiles from “any man [ish ish]” as taking vows like a Jew. For in such a case it says (Me’ila 7b), regarding the peace offerings of a Jew, that one may not benefit from them by Torah law even though they are not subject to misuse. One must say: since [gentiles’ consecrated animals] have no sanctity with regard to piggul, notar and impurity, they also have no sanctity with regard to benefit by Torah law.
gershom:a3.1: One is not liable for misuse: of them by Torah law; even so, one may not benefit from them, by rabbinic law.
rashi:a6.1: And he derives notar by “profane,” “profane” from impurity: that consecrated items of gentiles are not subject to [the prohibition of] notar.
rashi:a6.2: And it is written regarding notar: “But everyone who eats it shall bear his iniquity, because he has profaned the holy item of the Lord” (Leviticus 19:8): just as the profaning stated regarding impurity concerns Jews and not gentiles, so too the profaning stated here concerns Jews and not gentiles.
tosafot:a6.1: And he derives notar by “profane,” “profane” from impurity: and regarding impurity it is written “the children of Israel,” and not gentiles. The Maharam asked: Let us instead derive notar by “profane,” “profane” from an impure [priest] who performed the service in impurity. For it says in the second chapter of Zevaḥim (15b) [that the exclusion of] consecrated items of gentiles [from being] offered in impurity [is unnecessary], as it says there: “Rather, to exclude gentiles? Now, the frontplate does not effect acceptance [for them], as the Master said: For gentiles, whether unwittingly or intentionally, it is not accepted; will it be offered in impurity?” One can answer: it is more fitting to derive it from impurity, [since they are written] in one verse, as is stated in Zevaḥim, chapter Beit Shammai (45b), where Levi taught: “From where [is it derived] that the verse speaks also of disqualification by time? The verse states: ‘That they not profane the holy items of the children of Israel’: the verse speaks of two profanations, one the disqualification of notar and one the disqualification of impurity.”
rashi:a8.1: Now we explain the whole baraita, and it teaches: “And one does not make teruma” [the printed Rashi reads “teruma” here; the daf reads “substitution”]; and what is the reason one does not make substitution?
rashi:a9.1: This is the reading: “That substitution of an animal is juxtaposed with the animal tithe”: as we say below, at the end of our chapter (Temurah 13a): “But isn’t the tithe included among the other consecrated items, etc.? Why was it singled out? To juxtapose [the others] to it and tell you: just as the tithe is an individual’s offering and is subject to substitution, so too every individual’s offering is subject to substitution,” to exclude communal offerings.
rashi:a9.2: The animal tithe is juxtaposed with the grain tithe: as we say in Bekhorot (53b): “You shall surely tithe [aser te’aser]”: the verse speaks of two tithes, one the animal tithe and one the grain tithe.
rashi:a9.3: And regarding the grain tithe it is written: “For the tithe of the children of Israel” (Numbers 18:24): which implies the children of Israel and not gentiles. So too regarding the animal tithe: Jews and not gentiles. And just as we say regarding the animal tithe, Jews and not gentiles, so too let us say regarding the substitution of an animal, since they are all juxtaposed with one another. From here it is derived that consecrated items of gentiles are not subject to substitution.
tosafot:a9.1: And the grain tithe: it is written “the children of Israel,” and not gentiles. This is Rabbi Shimon, who holds this exposition, but the Rabbis disagree with him; and the first version belongs to the Rabbis.
gershom:a4.1: Another version: the substitution of an animal is juxtaposed with the animal tithe: for regarding the animal tithe it is written, “He shall not inquire whether it is good or bad, neither shall he substitute it,” and regarding the substitution of an animal it is written, “He shall not exchange it, nor substitute it.” And the animal tithe is juxtaposed with the grain tithe, as it says in the chapter Ma’aser Behema: “You shall surely tithe [aser te’aser]”: the verse speaks of two tithes, one the grain tithe and one the animal tithe.
rashi:a10.1: Homeborn: this is a Jew; and a gentile does not bring libations at all.
rashi:a10.2: One might have thought that his burnt offering should not require libations: even from communal [funds].
rashi:a10.3: The verse states “so”: for “so” indicates an indispensable requirement, that they certainly require libations, and from communal [funds]. And according to the other version, which is written in the books, and in which we do not read “for them” [in the baraita], it means this: one who is homeborn, that is, a Jew, brings libations even by themselves, and a gentile does not bring libations by themselves. One might have thought that his burnt offering should not require libations; the verse states “so,” and it is indispensable: his offering certainly requires libations, even from his own [funds], for we accept from him the money for the libations.
rashi:a11.1: This is the reading: “What is the reason? ‘To the Lord’ is written regarding them,” and we do not read “holy to the Lord.” So I found in Zevaḥim, in the chapter Beit Shammai (45a): “What is the reason? ‘To the Lord’ is written regarding them,” regarding consecrated items of gentiles, as it is written: “Whosoever he be of the house of Israel … that brings his offering,” etc. We establish this verse as referring to gentiles, who vow vow offerings and gift offerings like Jews; and at the end of the verse “to the Lord” is written, as it is stated: “which are brought to the Lord,” to tell you that we treat them by the law of other consecrated items: one is liable for misusing them, and one is liable for them for piggul, etc.
gershom:a5.1: What is the reason? “To the Lord” is written regarding it: as it is written, “any of their vows … which are brought to the Lord.” Therefore one is liable for misusing them.
tosafot:a12.1: What is teruma? Inherent sanctity: And if you say: But it is said that the warning against intentionally misusing [consecrated property] is derived by “sin,” “sin” from teruma; we should have said there, as here: just as teruma has inherent sanctity, so the warning of misuse should apply only to items consecrated for the altar. Yet we hold that the warning of misuse applies even to items consecrated for Temple maintenance, as we learned (Keritot 13b): “There is one who eats a single eating and is liable for it four sin offerings and one guilt offering,” and it counts consecrated items [there; the printed text adds a parenthetical about “an ox and a donkey” whose sense is unclear]. Likewise several expositions in the last chapter of Me’ila (18b), [about one who] damaged [an item] and benefited, and an agent who carried out his agency, which we derive from teruma; we should have said that they do not apply to items consecrated for Temple maintenance. One can answer: the reason we exclude items consecrated for Temple maintenance here is that “to the Lord” is written here.
rashi:a14.1: But there is substitution, which is a prohibition that does not involve an action: for the matter depends on speech.
tosafot:a14.1: But there is substitution, a prohibition that does not involve an action, and he is flogged: And if you say: Why does it not likewise challenge from one who defames [his bride] and from conspiring witnesses, whose prohibitions do not involve an action, and one is flogged? One can say: it did not want to challenge from those, since lashes are written explicitly for them in the Torah. And if you say: In Tractate Makkot (4b), where Ulla says one is flogged for a prohibition that does not involve an action and derives it from one who defames, the Gemara challenges: “What about one who defames? He is [also subject to] a fine.” Let it say: one who takes an oath, or one who effects substitution, or one of the others in our passage will prove [the point]. One can say: it is indeed so, but the answer given [there] is also sound; or perhaps the cases here are not similar to those there. And if you say: When the Gemara challenges here, “But there is substitution, which is a prohibition that does not involve an action,” let it answer that through his speech an action was done, as it says below. One can say: it indeed could have answered so, but the answer it gave is also sound.
rashi:a15.1: It is Rabbi Yehuda: who discusses this matter below.
rashi:a18.1: If he did not perform an action he is exempt, except for one who takes an oath, etc.: for they are flogged even though they perform no action, as is explained below.
rashi:a18.2: Using the name: using the name of the Holy One, Blessed be He.
gershom:a6.1: And one who curses another using the name: [the name] of the Holy [One]. And likewise one who separates teruma before the first fruits: this does not refer to one who actually separates it, which would be an action of consecrating teruma, but, for example, to one who set his eyes on this side [of the produce] as teruma. [On 3b:] Say that he is not cleared at all, even by the court.
tosafot:a18.1: Also one who separates teruma before the first fruits: below (4a) it explains the reason, that the verse states: “You shall not delay to offer of your fullness and of your outflow” [Exodus 22:28]: “your fullness” is the first fruits, and “your outflow” is teruma, and the Merciful One said, “You shall not delay.” The Sifrei explains another reason: the first fruits should come first, since they have four names. Rashi cites it below (Temurah 4a, s.v. mipnei).
rashi:a19.1: One who takes an oath, from where do we derive: that he is flogged?
rashi:b1.1: They do not clear him: as it is written, “For the Lord will not clear him.”
rashi:b2.1: [He cannot be absolved] at all: that the lower court does not flog him [to clear him].
rashi:b3.1: We found an oath in vain: as it is written, “that takes His name in vain” (Exodus 20:7); this is an oath in vain, such as one who swears to alter what is known to people.
rashi:b3.2: A false oath: it explains below what the case is.
rashi:b3.3: From where do we derive it: that he is flogged for it?
gershom:b1.1: We found an oath in vain: that he is flogged. An oath in vain is one who swears to alter what is known to people: he said of a stone pillar that it is of gold, or swore [that he saw something absurd, such as]: “If I did not see a snake like the beam of an olive press.”
rashi:b4.1: He performed an action: and by right he should be flogged, since he ate and so performed an action.
rashi:b4.2: And he did not eat: for this is not an action.
rashi:b4.3: Is that individual flogged?: said in astonishment.
rashi:b5.1: Because it is an uncertain forewarning: for if they warn him, “Take care to eat the loaf about which you swore,” he can say, “This warning gives me no cause for concern, as I still have time,” and so all day long. And even when the day has passed he can say, “I forgot, and remembered neither the oath nor the warning,” and he is not flogged.
gershom:b2.1: Because it is an uncertain forewarning: for when they warn him, “Take care to eat it today,” he says, “I will do so when I am free, and there is still much time in the day”; and if the day passed and he did not eat it, he can say, “I forgot it.” For any forewarning that is not at the time of the act, such as this one, is an uncertain forewarning and is not considered a forewarning, since he can say, “I forgot the warning.”
rashi:b6.1: Let it be with “I ate” or “I did not eat”: that is, let the false oath be where one swore that he did not eat and he had eaten, or that he ate and he had not eaten. Here there is no action at all, since he swore about the past.
gershom:b3.1: Rather, Rabbi Abbahu said: let it be: that he is flogged for a false oath where he said, “An oath that I ate,” and he had not eaten, or, “An oath that I did not eat,” and he had eaten before the oath; and what was before the oath is not an action [connected to the oath].
rashi:b7.1: And what is different about “I ate” or “I did not eat”: that is, why specifically does it exclude “I will eat” and he did not eat from lashes, more than “I ate” or “I did not eat”? In both there is no action at all.
gershom:b4.1: And what is different: with “I will eat” and he did not eat, you said that since it involves no action he is not flogged; and what is different with “I ate” or “I did not eat,” that you said that although it involves no action he is flogged?
rashi:b7.2: A false oath similar to an oath in vain: as was derived above from “in vain,” “in vain,” twice.
rashi:b7.3: Just as an oath in vain is about the past: for when one swears about a stone pillar that it is of silver, that is about the past, since in the past, before he swore, it was a stone, as it is now. And just as for an oath in vain he is flogged, as we said above, “the lower court flogs him and clears him,” so too a false oath about the past, that is, “I ate” or “I did not eat,” to exclude “I will eat” and he did not eat, which concerns the future.
gershom:b5.1: The Torah explicitly included: a false oath, as it is written “in vain,” “in vain,” twice. Therefore we require a false oath similar to an oath in vain: just as an oath in vain is about the past, where one swears to alter what is known to people, saying of a stone pillar that it is of gold, and lies about what has passed, knowing that it was not so, so too for a false oath we require one about the past, that is, “I ate” or “I did not eat,” which concerns the past. [The printed text of this note carries several bracketed corrections; this rendering follows the corrected reading.]
rashi:b8.1: An oath that I will not eat this loaf, etc.: for he swore three times that he would not eat that loaf.
rashi:b8.2: He is liable for only one: as we say in Shevuot that an oath does not take effect upon an oath.
rashi:b8.3: And this is the oath of utterance: of which the verse says, “to utter with the lips, to do evil or to do good” (Leviticus 5:4). This is the oath of utterance: he utters with his lips that he will not eat that loaf, but he did not rob his fellow of anything. But for the oath of testimony and the oath of deposit, one brings [an offering] for intentional violation as for unwitting violation: a guilt offering [for the oath of deposit].
tosafot:b8.1: An oath that I will not eat this loaf, an oath that I will not eat it, and he ate it, he is liable for only one: It specifically put “an oath that I will not eat” first. For had he said, “An oath that I will not eat it,” and then, “An oath that I will not eat,” he would be liable for two: “that I will not eat it” implies the whole of it, and when he then says, “An oath that I will not eat,” it implies [not eating] at all [even a little]. And in Shevuot (27b) it explains why it teaches “that I will not eat it” twice.
gershom:b6.1: He is liable for only one: for an oath does not take effect upon an oath.
rashi:b8.4: To exclude what?: that one is not liable to lashes for its intentional violation.
rashi:b8.5: Is it not to exclude “I ate” or “I did not eat”?: that although it is an oath of utterance, he is not flogged, since “to do evil or to do good” is written, which implies the future, excluding the past, such as “I ate” or “I did not eat.” And [if so,] what then is the case of the false oath?
rashi:b9.1: He does not bring an offering: because “to do evil or to do good” is stated with regard to the offering; but in any case he is liable to lashes for it, similar to an oath in vain.
gershom:b7.1: But “I ate” or “I did not eat”: he does not bring an offering, but he is flogged.
rashi:b9.2: Who said: [Rabbi Yishmael,] in Tractate Shevuot (25a): one is liable only for the future to come.
rashi:b10.1: This is an oath in vain: this “This is an oath in vain, etc.” is the latter clause of that mishna cited above.
gershom:b8.1: But “I ate” or “I did not eat”: he brings an offering, and he is flogged.
rashi:b12.1: And the first clause is not to exclude “I ate” or “I did not eat”: for “I ate” or “I did not eat” he is certainly liable to an offering for its unwitting violation.
gershom:b9.1: And the first clause is not to exclude “I ate” or “I did not eat” from an offering, but to exclude “I will eat” and he did not eat: from an offering.
rashi:b13.1: And what is different: that it excludes “I will eat” and he did not eat from an offering, while it includes “I ate” or “I did not eat,” from the latter clause, as liable to an offering? It answers: it stands to reason that the first clause excludes “I will eat” and he did not eat.
tosafot:b13.1: And what is different: Rashi explained: what is different, that it excludes “I will eat” and he did not eat from an offering, and includes “I ate” or “I did not eat,” from the latter clause, as liable to an offering? This is not clear: if it says that it excludes “I will eat” and he did not eat, there is no difficulty at all; only if it had said the reverse would there be a difficulty. The Ri explained: what is different, that it explains [the mishna] according to Rabbi Akiva? Let it establish it according to Rabbi Yishmael, with the first clause excluding “I ate” or “I did not eat” from an offering and the latter clause excluding “I will eat” and he did not eat from lashes. And it answers: since it deals with the future, etc.
gershom:b10.1: And what is different: that this one excludes [the future].
rashi:b13.2: Since it deals with the future: for it teaches “an oath that I will not eat it,” and it excludes the future, such as “I will eat” and he did not eat.
rashi:b13.3: But if it deals with the future, would it exclude the past?: said in astonishment; for example, “I ate” or “I did not eat.”
gershom:b11.1: Because it deals with the future: with “an oath that I will not eat,” it excludes the future, an oath “that I will eat” and he did not eat. But “I ate,” which concerns the past, it does not exclude; rather, he is flogged for it, in accordance with Rabbi Abbahu.
rashi:b14.1: Do not teach “and one who effects substitution”: among the other prohibitions that do not involve an action.
rashi:b14.2: For by his speech he performs an action: for he makes non-sacred [animals] into consecrated ones.
gershom:b12.1: Because by his speech he performed an action: for he consecrates a non-sacred animal. “That you may fear this name”: it enters our mind that this “that you may fear the name” means that you should fear it so as not to curse your fellow with it, and hafla’a is written regarding it, which is lashes.
tosafot:b15.1: And one who curses another using the name, from where do we derive it: “If you will not observe to perform … then [the Lord] will make wondrous.” Its warning is from here: “You shall not curse the deaf”; alternatively, from this verse itself.
rashi:b15.1: If you will not observe to perform, etc.: up to “that you may fear the name,” that he should fear not to utter the name in vain; and one who curses another using the name likewise utters it in vain. And it is written, “Then the Lord will make your plagues wondrous,” that he will receive blows, and that is lashes.
rashi:b16.1: Even a true oath: that the verse warns that one should not make even a true oath with the name of Heaven, and if he does, “Then the Lord will make your plagues wondrous,” that he receives lashes.
gershom:b13.1: Say that this “that you may fear the name” is not about one who curses another using the name, but that you should fear it so as not to swear by His name, even truthfully.
rashi:b16.2: It is written explicitly: that it is permitted to do so.
rashi:b17.1: To appease his fellow: so that he will not claim money from him; but he should be flogged, since he brings himself to an oath.
gershom:b14.1: Say that this “The oath of the Lord shall be between them both” does not mean that it is permitted ab initio to swear truthfully. Rather, an oath is needed in order to appease the mind of the owner. And say: it is better that he appease him with money and not with an oath, and if [the owner] does not want money but an oath, he swears to him to appease him, but he is flogged for the true oath. And say that this is what “that you may fear the name” comes for, and not for one who curses another using the name.
rashi:b17.2: And by His name you shall swear: that it is permitted to make a true oath.
rashi:b18.1: To fulfill the mitzvot: so that he cannot retract, as it is stated, “I have sworn, and have confirmed it,” etc. And for this the verse “and by His name you shall swear” is needed, to teach us that one who swears to fulfill a mitzva is permitted to do so.
gershom:b15.1: That you cannot say: that he is flogged for a true oath, for another verse is written that permits it, as it is written, “and by His name you shall swear.” [The Gemara answers:] Say that “and by His name you shall swear,” which permits swearing, permits it only for a matter of a mitzva, in order to spur himself on, in accordance with what Rav Giddel said that Rav said.
rashi:b18.2: But another verse is written, “and by His name you shall swear”: two verses are written with “and by His name you shall swear,” one in [the portion of] Va’etḥanan and one in Ekev. One is needed for one who swears to fulfill a mitzva, and the other for a true oath.
gershom:b16.1: But another verse is written, “and by His name you shall swear”: for “and by His name you shall swear” is written twice, [one for the teaching of Rav Giddel] and one to permit even an ordinary true oath; and so “that you may fear” remains free for one who curses another using the name.
gershom:b17.1: Another version: that teaching of Rav Giddel is derived from “and to Him you shall cleave.” [Then why do I need “and by His name you shall swear”? If it is not needed for the oath of judges, which is permitted and is derived from “the oath of the Lord,” apply it to an ordinary oath that is not before judges; and if it is not needed for an oath for a mitzva, which is derived from “and to Him you shall cleave,” apply it to a true oath (it seems it should read: a true oath that is optional). If so, this verse “that you may fear the name” perforce comes for one who curses another.]
rashi:b19.1: Rather, for what does it come: this “If you will not observe,” etc.
rashi:b19.2: For one who curses another using the name: that he is certainly flogged, even though he performed no action.
rashi:b19.3: The name of Heaven in vain: but one who curses another using the name would not be flogged. And it answers him: is it not all the more so?
gershom:b18.1: And say that this “that you may fear” comes to make one who utters the name [of Heaven] in vain liable, and not one who curses.
rashi:b20.1: For where he commits two prohibitions, lashes should not suffice for him: and even though he was flogged, he has still not been atoned for through lashes alone.
gershom:b19.1: This you cannot say: for is one who curses another using the name any less than one who utters the name of Heaven in vain? For one who curses using the name commits two prohibitions: he utters the name in vain in order to curse his fellow, and moreover he curses his fellow; he is certainly not less, [but more severe]. This is what is difficult for us: let us say that for one who utters the name of Heaven in vain, lashes suffice for him, and that is why “make wondrous” is written; but for one who curses another using the name, lashes should not suffice, since he did two [things].
